content: Standard multimeters are capable of measuring voltage, current, and resistance. They are categorized into two main types: analog multimeters, which use a moving pointer to display readings, and digital multimeters (DMMs), which provide numerical readouts. They are widely used to diagnose electrical issues in various devices, including batteries, motor controls, household appliances, power supplies, and wiring systems. Multimeters are available at a broad range of price points, from inexpensive models costing under $10 to advanced models exceeding $5000. Capacitance (farads) Frequency (hertz) Duty cycle (percentage) Temperature (Celsius or Fahrenheit) Conductance (siemens) Inductance (henrys) Audio signal levels (decibels) Digital multimeters often include additional features, such as: Light intensity pH levels (acidity/alkalinity) Wind speed Relative humidity Resolution Digital Multimeters The resolution of a digital multimeter is expressed in terms of digits. For example, a 5½-digit multimeter displays five full digits (0–9) and one half digit, which can only display 0 or 1. This allows the meter to display values up to 199,999. A 3¾-digit multimeter, on the other hand, can display values up to 3,999 or 5,999, depending on the manufacturer. Analog Multimeters The resolution of an analog multimeter is limited by factors such as the width of the pointer, scale printing accuracy, and user interpretation. Errors can arise from parallax (viewing angle), miscounting scale divisions, or poor eyesight. Mirrored scales and larger meter movements can improve resolution, but analog meters typically achieve an equivalent resolution of 2½ to 3 digits. Accuracy Digital multimeters generally provide higher accuracy than analog models. Analog multimeters typically have an accuracy of 3–5%, while portable digital multimeters can achieve accuracies of 0. Bench-top digital multimeters may offer accuracies as high as ±0.01%, and laboratory-grade instruments can achieve accuracies in the parts-per-million range. Sensitivity and Input Impedance The accuracy of a multimeter can be affected by the current it draws from the circuit under test. Digital multimeters and analog meters with electronic amplifiers typically have high input impedance (e.g., 1 MΩ or 10 MΩ), minimizing circuit loading. Traditional analog multimeters, however, draw current directly from the circuit, with input impedance varying based on the meter's sensitivity and selected range. For example, a meter with a sensitivity of 20,000 ohms/volt would have an input resistance of 2 MΩ on the 100-volt range. High-sensitivity meters are essential for measuring low-impedance circuits without significantly affecting the circuit under test. Digital Multimeters (DMMs) Digital multimeters are preferred for their accuracy, durability, and additional features. In a DMM, the input signal is converted to a voltage, amplified, and displayed as a numerical value, eliminating parallax errors. Common features include: Analog Multimeters Analog multimeters use a moving-coil galvanometer to deflect a pointer across a scale. While less accurate than digital models, they are valued for their ability to display trends and rates of change. Some analog meters, such as vacuum tube voltmeters (VTVMs) or transistor voltmeters (TVMs), include amplifiers to increase input impedance and reduce circuit loading. Sensitivity is typically expressed in ohms per volt, with higher sensitivity meters drawing less current from the circuit under test. Probes Multimeters use various test probes to connect to the circuit under test. Common probe types include: Crocodile clips Retractable hook clips Pointed probes Probes are attached to insulated leads, which connect to the multimeter via banana jacks, BNC connectors, or other interfaces. Safety Many multimeters include fuses to protect against overcurrent, but these fuses often only safeguard the highest current range. Digital multimeters are categorized based on their intended application, as defined by the CEN EN61010 standard: Category I: Low-current environments Category II: Residential branch circuits Category III: Permanently installed loads (e.g., distribution panels) Category IV: High-current environments (e.g., service entrances) Each category specifies maximum transient voltages for the meter's measuring ranges and includes protections against overcurrent faults. History The multimeter was invented in the 1920s to support the growing use of radio receivers and vacuum tube electronics. As technology has advanced, multimeters have become more sophisticated, often supplemented by specialized tools for specific applications. For example, modern technicians may use network analyzers to test parameters beyond the capabilities of a general-purpose multimeter.
